extracted.intended_audience: consumers and the general public (people interested in consumer safety and correcting misconceptions about tort cases)
extracted.subtask_description: Explains the facts of the 1992 Liebeck v. McDonald's case to correct misconceptions and show why the case was not frivolous, by listing evidence presented at trial and explaining its significance for consumer safety and corporate responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangerous serving temperature
rubrics_metrics.description: McDonald’s operations manual required the franchisee to hold its coffee at 180 to 190 degrees Fahrenheit; coffee at that temperature, if spilled, causes third-degree burns in three to seven seconds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use objective measurements (company policy, temperature specs) and scientific/medical timing of burns to evaluate whether a served product is unreasonably dangerous; expert testimony on thermal injury thresholds strengthens this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity of the plaintiff’s injuries
rubrics_metrics.description: Mrs. Liebeck suffered third-degree burns and required skin grafts on her inner thighs and elsewhere; her clothing (sweatpants) absorbed the coffee and kept it against her skin, worsening injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess actual medical outcomes (degree of burns, need for surgery/grafts, scarring, lost income) rather than relying on caricatures of the incident; severe physical harm supports a non-frivolous claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Company knowledge of the risk
rubrics_metrics.description: McDonald’s admitted it had known about the risk of serious burns from its scalding hot coffee for more than 10 years; the company had received more than 700 previous reports of injury from its coffee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior reports, internal admissions, or corporate records indicating awareness of a hazard are strong evidence of corporate culpability and negate claims that harms were unforeseeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to warn consumers
rubrics_metrics.description: McDonald’s admitted it did not warn customers of the nature and extent of this risk and could offer no explanation as to why it did not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lack of adequate warnings where a known, non-obvious danger exists is a significant factor in evaluating negligence/liability; consider whether consumers were reasonably aware of the risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern of prior incidents and settlements
rubrics_metrics.description: McDonald’s had received more than 700 reports of injury including reports of third-degree burns and had paid settlements in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pattern of similar incidents and prior settlements indicates systemic risk and failure to remedy a dangerous practice; use frequency and past payouts to assess reasonableness of corporate conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credible expert testimony establishing hazard
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts testified that the risk of harm was unacceptable: the chairman of mechanical/biomechanical engineering at UT and the editor-in-chief of the Journal of Burn Care and Rehabilitation testified about burn risks and unacceptability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent, authoritative expert testimony on engineering, biomechanics, or medical effects is persuasive evidence of unreasonably dangerous product/service conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Company’s statistical minimization vs human impact
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert witness for the company testified that the number of burns was insignificant compared to the billions of cups served each year; jurors noted that statistical rarity ignores the individual victims behind each number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize defenses that rely solely on statistical rarity; evaluating corporate conduct should weigh individual harms and corporate duty, not just frequency relative to volume of sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality assurance admissions about product unfitness
rubrics_metrics.description: McDonald’s quality assurance manager testified that McDonald’s coffee, at the temperature at which it was poured into Styrofoam cups, was not fit for consumption because it would burn the mouth and throat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissions from internal QA or operations personnel that a product is unfit for consumption/usage are powerful indicators of defectiveness or dangerous practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness of settlement offers and corporate refusal
rubrics_metrics.description: Mrs. Liebeck offered to settle the case for $20,000 to cover medical expenses and lost income; McDonald’s never offered more than $800, leading to trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare plaintiff settlement demands to actual damages and corporate settlement behavior; disproportionate refusal to offer reasonable compensation can support punitive or deterrence-minded verdicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of fault and punitive damages rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury found Mrs. Liebeck partially at fault (reducing compensatory damages) but awarded punitive damages to punish McDonald’s 'callous disregard for the safety of the people'; a judge later reduced the punitive award substantially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both comparative fault and the reasons for punitive awards: partial plaintiff fault does not preclude punitive damages when corporate conduct shows willful or reckless disregard; judicial review can modify excessive punitive awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer unawareness of the extent of the risk
rubrics_metrics.description: McDonald’s admitted consumers were unaware of the extent of the risk of serious burns from spilled coffee served at McDonald’s then-required temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether ordinary consumers would appreciate the specific danger; lack of consumer knowledge about magnitude of risk supports duty to warn or to mitigate the hazard.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-hand juror assessment and perception of corporate attitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: At least one juror said the company wasn’t taking the injuries seriously and others said the facts were 'overwhelmingly against the company'—jurors reacted to corporate indifference despite evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juror testimony about how evidence was perceived (e.g., corporate callousness) can illuminate why a jury may impose punitive measures; persuasive narratives of corporate disregard matter in trial outcomes.
